summary: Clarifies how TRILL switches on a shared link choose which one handles traffic for each VLAN, the "Appointed Forwarder" mechanism. The goal is at most one switch handling native traffic per VLAN. It updates RFC 6325 and RFC 7177 and replaces RFC 6439.

plainLanguage.summary: Several TRILL switches can sit on the same network link. Each VLAN on that link needs just one of them to handle the end stations' ordinary frames, so that frames cannot loop. This document explains how that switch is chosen, how the others are kept out of the way, and how they learn quickly that a port has gone down.

subtitle: How TRILL switches on one link agree which of them handles the end stations' traffic in each VLAN.

tldr.problem: Several TRILL switches can be attached to the same network link. If more than one of them handles the ordinary frames of end stations on that link, frames can loop, so each VLAN needs a single switch in charge of it.
tldr.mechanism: The link's Designated RBridge appoints one switch as the Appointed Forwarder for each VLAN and tells the others in link-scoped link-state advertisements or in Hellos. A switch that hears a competing claim for the same VLAN stops handling native frames for that VLAN until a timer expires.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8139 replaces RFC 6439 and updates RFC 6325 and RFC 7177. It moves appointment data out of the small Hello message into link-scoped link-state advertisements and adds a fast Port-Shutdown notification.

facts.label: VLAN inhibition timers
facts.value: Up to 4,094 per link, at least 2 required

today: RFC 8139 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It replaced RFC 6439 and updates RFC 6325 and RFC 7177, so it is the current description of how TRILL switches on a link agree which one handles each VLAN.

sections.title: One Switch in Charge of Each VLAN
sections.content:
TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) is a link-state routing protocol for Layer 2 networks. Devices that implement it are called TRILL switches or RBridges (Routing Bridges). TRILL carries traffic between end stations inside a TRILL Data packet that carries a hop count, which keeps forwarding safe even while temporary loops exist.

TRILL supports multi-access links, where several end stations and several RBridges are attached to the same link. On such a link the native frames, the ordinary Ethernet frames that come from and go to end stations, must be handled by one RBridge for each VLAN. That RBridge is the Appointed Forwarder. Two Appointed Forwarders for the same VLAN on one link could form a loop in which part of the loop has no TRILL hop count to stop it.

This document updates the mechanism originally given in RFC 6325 and frees it from the size limit of the TRILL Hello message. It also adds optional ways to detect inconsistent VLAN to label mappings on a link, to report a port shutdown quickly, and to shorten the period during which a switch is inhibited.
sections.plainLanguage: Several TRILL switches can sit on the same network link. Each VLAN on that link needs one of them to handle the end stations' ordinary frames, so that frames cannot loop. This document explains how that switch is chosen and how the others are kept out of the way.

sections.title: How Appointments Are Made
sections.content:
The Appointed Forwarder on a link for VLAN-x is the RBridge that ingresses native frames from that link and egresses native frames to it in VLAN-x. By default the DRB (Designated RBridge), the RBridge elected on the link to handle link-wide decisions, is in charge of native traffic for every VLAN on the link. The DRB may appoint other RBridges that have ports on the link.

The DRB can appoint through two mechanisms. Method A puts Appointed Forwarders sub-TLVs, in the form of AppointmentBitmap or AppointmentList APPsub-TLVs, into E-L1CS FS-LSPs, which are link-scoped IS-IS link-state advertisements. Method B puts Appointed Forwarders sub-TLVs into a TRILL Hello sent on the Designated VLAN. When the DRB sends appointments in a Hello it must send all of them in that one Hello, and any appointment left out is revoked.

Each RBridge keeps two databases: an E-L1CS LSDB, which is semi-permanent and shows what each RBridge on the link would appoint if it were the DRB, and a Hello appointment database, which is reset by each Hello from the DRB that carries appointments. An RBridge is the Appointed Forwarder for a VLAN if either database says so. Because the E-L1CS method is RECOMMENDED and the Hello method is only needed for RBridges that do not support E-L1CS, the limit of about 1,000 bytes available for appointments in a Hello does not usually apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch elected to look after a link, called the Designated RBridge, names which switch handles each VLAN. It can send that information in link-state advertisements or in the short Hello messages. Each switch remembers both, and steps in only when one of them names it.

sections.title: The Inhibition Mechanism
sections.content:
Inhibition is the safety net that stops an RBridge from handling native frames on a link when it might conflict with another RBridge. Each RBridge keeps a DRB inhibition timer, a root bridge change inhibition timer, and up to 4,094 VLAN inhibition timers, one for each legal VLAN ID. The first two timers MUST be implemented, and at least two VLAN inhibition timers MUST be implemented, so that a switch which is the Appointed Forwarder for one VLAN can be timed separately from the rest.

An Appointed Forwarder is inhibited for VLAN-x when its DRB inhibition timer, its root bridge change inhibition timer, or its VLAN-x inhibition timer has not expired. While inhibited it ignores native frames arriving in VLAN-x, apart from learning their addresses, and it does not send decapsulated frames out to that link in VLAN-x. Inhibition has no effect on TRILL Data or TRILL IS-IS frames.

The root bridge change timer is set when the common spanning tree root bridge seen on a port changes. It defaults to 30 seconds and can be configured from 30 down to 0 seconds. Three optional optimizations let a switch end that inhibition early: when the root bridge changes to a lower priority, when only the priority part of the root Bridge ID changed, or when Hellos have been received from every RBridge that could see the old or the new root.
sections.plainLanguage: Inhibition is how a switch temporarily steps aside. It watches for signs that another switch on the link is handling the same VLAN, and stops moving end-station frames in that VLAN until its timers run out. The timers are per link and per VLAN, so one VLAN can be blocked without blocking the others.

sections.title: Port-Shutdown Messages
sections.content:
A TRILL switch normally learns that a neighbouring port has failed only after it misses a number of Hellos, which can take many seconds. The Port-Shutdown message reports such an event explicitly. It is an RBridge Channel message using RBridge Channel Protocol number 0x006, and its payload is a list of Port IDs for the ports that have failed or are being shut down.

For robustness a switch sends a configurable number of copies separated by a configurable interval: the default is two copies at 20 milliseconds, configurable from one to three copies and from 0 to 1,000 milliseconds. The message SHOULD be sent at priority 7 and SHOULD NOT be marked drop eligible. When a port failure is detected, the message is sent as a sequential unicast through the rest of the campus to every RBridge that had an adjacency with that port and that advertises support for the message.

On receipt a switch checks the ingress nickname against its own adjacencies and drops the adjacencies listed in the message. A shutdown planned within one second is announced by broadcast through the port being shut down. A port coming back up needs no message, because sending Hellos out of the port says so. This document also updates RFC 7177 so that receiving this message moves the affected adjacency to the Detect state.
sections.plainLanguage: When a port fails, the switch that owns it sends a short message naming the failed ports. Neighbours read it and drop their link to those ports straight away, instead of waiting for the usual timeout. The message is repeated a couple of times so that it is not lost.

sections.title: Encoding Appointments and VLAN Mappings
sections.content:
Four APPsub-TLVs are defined for use inside a TRILL GENINFO TLV in E-L1CS FS-LSPs. Type 17, AppointmentBitmap, names the RBridge being appointed and the first VLAN ID, then uses one bit per VLAN to list the VLANs it covers, which suits VLANs in a small numeric range. Type 18, AppointmentList, names the appointee and then lists 12-bit VLAN IDs one after another, which suits VLANs spread over a wide range. Type 19, FGL-VLAN-Bitmap, and type 20, FGL-VLAN-Pairs, let a switch advertise the mapping it applies between VLAN IDs and FGLs (Fine-Grained Labels).

The mapping matters because a VLAN ID in native traffic is carried inside a TRILL Data packet as an Inner.Label, and the mapping configured at the Appointed Forwarder is the mapping that is performed. Since the Appointed Forwarder for a VLAN can change, all TRILL switches on a link that are configured with a mapping SHOULD use the same one, and SHOULD advertise it so that consistency can be checked automatically. A switch SHOULD compare what it sees with its own mapping and alert the operator when they disagree, unless the disagreement lasts no longer than the switch's Holding Time.
sections.plainLanguage: The document defines four small sub-messages for carrying appointment and mapping data in link-state advertisements. One packs VLAN numbers into a row of bits, one lists them one by one, and two carry the label mapping that each switch uses for a VLAN.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document does not change the security considerations of the TRILL base protocol, which are described in Section 6 of RFC 6325.

Port-Shutdown messages are sent using the RBridge Channel facility. They SHOULD be secured with the RBridge Channel Header Extension, because an inadequately secured message of this kind is a potential denial-of-service vector. The E-L1CS FS-LSPs added by this document are a kind of IS-IS PDU, so they can be secured in the same way as Hellos and other IS-IS PDUs, by adding Authentication TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here changes the security rules of TRILL itself. The new port-shutdown message should be protected, because an attacker who forges one could make switches drop working links. The link-state advertisements can use the same authentication as ordinary IS-IS messages.

sections.title: Management and Configuration
sections.content:
The document mainly adds optional enhancements. The only configuration parameters it defines are for the Port-Shutdown message: PShutdownRepeat, whose default is 2 and whose range is 1 to 3, and PShutdownDelay, whose default is 20 milliseconds and whose range is 0 to 1,000 milliseconds.

SNMPv3 support is provided by the TRILL base protocol, and MIBs have been specified for RBridges and for TRILL operations, but they do not cover these parameters. YANG modules for TRILL are anticipated.

The document also changes earlier specifications. It makes support for E-L1CS FS-LSPs mandatory in the TRILL base protocol, updates RFC 7177 to treat a Port-Shutdown message as an adjacency event, and replaces RFC 6439, the earlier Appointed Forwarders document, with this one.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost nothing in TRILL needs configuring, and this document keeps it that way. It adds two settings for the port-shutdown message, the number of copies and the gap between them, and leaves the rest to the existing TRILL management objects.
